title: Backing communities, Catholic bishops sound alarm over Pax Silica's potential impact
summary: Catholic bishops are urging communities in Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino to display banners opposing large-scale mining and Pax Silica.

blocks.text: November 16, 2026 | 1:30pm

MANILA, Philippines — Several Catholic bishops have joined Indigenous Peoples and farming communities in Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino in condemning alleged human rights abuses linked to large-scale mining and calling for coordinated, peaceful protests ahead of US President Donald Trump's visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit on Tuesday, November 17.

In a November 12 pastoral statement, Bishop Jose Elmer Mangalinao of the Diocese of Bayombong urged parishes, schools, households and local government units across the two provinces to hang banners on Monday, November 16.
The efforts oppose large-scale mining and "Pax Silica," a US-led initiative he warned could intensify mineral extraction for military technology and artificial intelligence production.

"Nueva Vizcaya has long carried the heavy burden of large-scale, foreign-led mining. Our mountains, rivers, farms, forests, and communities have endured the costs of extraction: threatened livelihoods, damaged ecosystems, uncertain water sources, and the displacement and insecurity experienced by farming and Indigenous communities," Mangalinao's pastoral statement read.
These are not "abstract concerns," he said as they affect families who work the land and live on it.
He urged families, churches, schools and municipal halls to display tarpaulins, painted cloth or handwritten signs bearing messages against large-scale mining and Pax Silica.

"Let our churches, schools, homes, and communities raise this banner as a sign of faith, courage, and solidarity: that the land belongs to the people who live from it and care for it, and that no development is truly progress if it leaves communities displaced, impoverished, or silenced," he added.
Mangalinao said residents in Dupax del Norte and Kasibu have been experiencing harassment while defending their lands against foreign-led mining operations.
He warned that advancing Pax Silica without genuine consultation could worsen displacement, water insecurity and intimidation.

"If Pax Silica pushes forward without genuine consultation and strong protections, the same pattern may become worse: communities may face greater pressure to give up their land, while those who speak out may face more harassment and intimidation," the prelate said.

Mangalinao's pastoral call was also supported by Caritas Philippines President and Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) Episcopal Commission on Social Action, Justice and Peace Chair Bishop Gerardo Alminaza, as well as CBCP Episcopal Commission on Indigenous Peoples Chair Bishop Moises Cuevas.
The prelates expressed grave concern over community accounts of intimidation, violent dispersals, red-tagging and judicial harassment.
They also noted that local communities have questioned the validity of certain permits, Certificates of Non-Overlap and consent processes affecting their ancestral domains and watersheds.

"No promise of economic development can justify violations of human dignity, the disregard of Peoples' rights, or the destruction of the natural resources upon which communities depend," the prelates' statement read.

"The Church does not reject development. Rather, we champion authentic development that nurtures the whole human person, respects community dignity, protects the integrity of creation, and serves the common good," they added.
What is Pax Silica?
Pax Silica is a US-led initiative launched in December 2025 to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence infrastructure and critical minerals among participating countries.
In the Philippines, a major proposed project under the initiative is a high-tech manufacturing and innovation hub in New Clark City, Tarlac, within the Luzon Economic Corridor.
Critics have warned that the proposed hub could threaten agricultural livelihoods, ancestral lands and communities in Capas, Tarlac.

The Bases Conversion and Development Authority, however, has maintained that the project site is within areas designated for development and has assured residents that affected communities would receive assistance and relocation support.
